etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre, from Latin extendō (“I stretch out”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To possess a certain extent; to cover an amount of space.
(transitive) To cause to increase in extent.
(transitive) To cause to last for a longer period of time.
(transitive) To bestow; to offer; to impart; to apply.
To increase in quantity by weakening or adulterating additions.

quote.citation: 1894, Fred Grundy, “Management of Fall Pigs”, in The American Agriculturist Volume 54:
quote.text: The skim milk and middlings should be mixed in a tub or barrel, and, if the supply of milk is short , it may be extended with water.

quote.citation: 1897, Alonzo Lewis, James Robinson Newhall, History of Lynn, Essex County, Massachusetts, page 155:
quote.text: […]  the exalted morality of those virtuous brethren in the trade who, with consciences as weak as their own "extended" liquors, sought to convince him that to reduce the drink was a mercy to the poor deluded toper.

definitions.definition: (UK, law) To value, as lands taken by a writ of extent in satisfaction of a debt; to assign by writ of extent.
(object-oriented programming) Of a class: to be an extension or subtype of, or to be based on, a prototype or a more abstract class.
(intransitive, US, military) To reenlist for a further period.

quote.text: Two years later, back to amtracs, this time at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, and I liked it so much I extended.
